name: Periodic limb movement disorder
aliases: periodic limb movements of sleep disorder

reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Defined by periodic, stereotyped limb movements during sleep that fragment sleep and cause insomnia or daytime tiredness
The movements are typically extension of the big toe with ankle dorsiflexion, sometimes with knee and hip flexion, recurring at fairly regular intervals
Diagnosis requires polysomnography showing a raised periodic limb movement index together with a clinical sleep complaint
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so periodic movements accompanying restless legs syndrome, sleep apnoea, narcolepsy or certain medications do not qualify as periodic limb movement disorder
Periodic limb movements in sleep are common, increase with age and are frequently asymptomatic, so they must be distinguished from the disorder itself
Iron deficiency should be sought and corrected, as low iron stores aggravate the movements
When treatment is needed, approaches mirror those for restless legs syndrome, such as alpha-2-delta ligands or dopaminergic agents, with attention to iron status
reference.pathophysiology: Periodic limb movements in sleep are thought to reflect disinhibition of spinal and brainstem motor generators, linked to altered central dopaminergic transmission and influenced by brain iron availability, since iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis. The same mechanisms underlie restless legs syndrome, with which the movements overlap. Periodic limb movement disorder is diagnosed only when these movements themselves disrupt sleep and no other disorder or drug better explains the picture.
additionalDifferentials: Restless legs syndrome with periodic limb movements
Obstructive sleep apnoea with movement-related arousals
Medication-induced movements, for example from antidepressants
additionalInvestigations: Overnight polysomnography with limb electromyography to quantify the periodic limb movement index and associated arousals
Assessment for restless legs syndrome symptoms to avoid double-labelling
Serum ferritin and iron studies to detect iron deficiency
Review of medications that can provoke the movements, notably antidepressants
redFlags: Excessive daytime sleepiness with driving or occupational risk
Features suggesting nocturnal seizures rather than periodic movements
Neurological signs pointing to a myelopathy or neuropathy
reference.prognosis: When a genuine disorder is confirmed and contributors such as iron deficiency or offending drugs are addressed, sleep and daytime symptoms usually improve; the movements themselves tend to persist and increase with age but are often asymptomatic.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the disorder from the incidental finding of periodic limb movements without a clinical sleep complaint
Labelling it as periodic limb movement disorder when restless legs syndrome or sleep apnoea is the real cause
Failing to check and treat iron deficiency
Overlooking antidepressants and other drugs that exacerbate the movements
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Identify and correct iron deficiency with iron replacement, since low brain iron availability aggravates the movements through impaired dopaminergic transmission
Review and withdraw or substitute provoking medications, notably antidepressants and dopamine antagonists
Treat any primary contributor rather than the movements alone, managing coexisting restless legs syndrome, sleep apnoea or narcolepsy
Offer a dopaminergic agent or an alpha-2-delta ligand (gabapentinoid) for a confirmed disorder that genuinely disrupts sleep
Advise sleep hygiene and reduction of caffeine, alcohol and nicotine
Confirm the diagnosis with polysomnography and monitor treatment response, recognising that asymptomatic periodic limb movements do not require treatment
